newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD's Schroeder backs EMU, doubts timing.
newsitem.headline: German SPD's Schroeder backs EMU, doubts timing.

text.p: Gerhard Schroeder, a leading candidate to challenge Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Germany's general election next year, said on Wednesday he supported Europe's single currency but doubted it should start so soon.

Schroeder, now competing with Social Democratic Party (SPD) chairman Oskar Lafontaine to become the opposition's standard bearer, told the weekly Die Zeit that Germany's tradition of stability was the most important issue to consider.

The Lower Saxony state premier denied being a Euro-sceptic but said the EU's planned economic and monetary union (EMU), which is debated far less widely in Germany than in other European countries, must be a subject for open discussion.

"The euro is a reasonable thing in principle, I just have my doubts about the timing," he said in the interview due to appear in Thursday's edition of Die Zeit. The single currency is scheduled to be launched in 1999.

"Whoever weakens the criteria," he said, referring to the Maastricht treaty's deficit and debt targets, "stokes fear of a soft currency. The voters will punish anyone who does not take seriously the stability culture that has developed here."

Schroeder, who supports strict adherence to the budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product, said the exact numbers involved were less important than the concept of stability which they represented.

"Don't bother me with these strict fiscal criteria," he said. "The catastrophe does not start at a 3.1 percent budget deficit or stop at 2.9 percent. This overlooks the fact we have a culture of stability in Germany."
Schroeder said the SPD should wait until April 1998, one month after he runs for reelection in his state, to decide whether he or Lafontaine should challenge Kohl.
He said he would pull out of the race if he scored two or more percentage points below his 1994 state election result of 44.3 percent.
As for his plans for debating the euro in a national campaign, he said: "We will not run a campaign about this by putting up posters saying we are for or against it.
"I'm not ready to be pushed into a corner as an anti-European. I am asking for nothing more than adherence to the conditions the government itself set up. That must be possible."
